question: How does sugar move across the Atlantic and become a plantation crop — and why does Europe's sugar trade pass from Venice and Antwerp to Brazil and Amsterdam?
summary: The sixteenth century is the century in which sugar changes continent. The Atlantic islands (Madeira, the Canaries, São Tomé) prove the formula and then are overtaken; the Caribbean island of Hispaniola gets cane in 1493, its first mills with state loans and Canary sugar-masters, and its first African slaves; Brazil, from the 1520s, becomes 'the Brazilian century for sugar' ([[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[te1]], [[o2]], [[l2]], [[o3]], [[ec3]]). The Mediterranean industry fades and Venice loses its place as Europe's entrepôt ([[w2]]).

Those who handle the sugar change too. Antwerp, which had nineteen refineries by about 1550, is sacked in 1576; Amsterdam, which had three or four in 1595, has over sixty by 1661 ([[ec5]], [[c1]], [[ec7]]). The Dutch fight the Portuguese for the sugar coast of Brazil, and when they lose it they will teach the English and French the methods ([[c4]], [[ec8]], [[b1]]). England, meanwhile, already has the sweet tooth: sugar is the main marker of rank at Elizabeth's table, and by 1591 it is cheaper in London than in Lisbon ([[e2]], [[c2]], [[l3]]).

China is the counter-example: the same century sees a large Chinese sugar economy in Fujian and Guangdong, a Dutch trade in Chinese sugar that grows with the war in Brazil, and the first Chinese illustrations of a two-roller crusher and of claying ([[ec6]], [[ec9]], [[te4]], [[te2]]). What the folio shows is not that Europe invented plantation sugar from nothing, but that it combined Mediterranean sugar-making, Atlantic geography, African slaves and Dutch commerce into something that reaches further than any earlier system.

themes.title: From islands to continent
text: Madeira, the Canaries and São Tomé show the plantation pattern at small scale (settlers, Italian finance, forest cleared for fuel, mills); Hispaniola and Brazil make it large. The folio's numbers (arrobas, mills, engenhos) trace the shift.

themes.title: Slavery arrives as the labour system
text: Mixed free and enslaved labour on the Canaries gives way to African slavery in Santo Domingo and then in Brazil. The Indigenous population of the islands has collapsed and Africans are shipped to work in the mines and mills.

themes.title: The refiners' ladder: Venice, Antwerp, Amsterdam
text: Control of sugar's refining and sale passes from one commercial capital to the next as war reshapes who can move cargo: the Venetian entrepôt, the Antwerp refineries, then Amsterdam's. The Dutch revolt, Philip II's claim to Portugal and the Brazilian war are the political side of the same shift.

themes.title: Sugar as taste, rank and teeth
text: Sugar sculptures at the Elizabethan court and in Fuzhou, the first cookbook complaints that sugar is overused, and the first reports of black teeth show sugar becoming social before it is cheap.

themes.title: China and Asia: a parallel system
text: Chinese sugar travels to Japan with the Portuguese, and the Dutch make Taiwan a sugar island; the Ming and early Qing technical books record the crusher and clay-refining methods.

turning_points.text: Skilled sugar-masters from the Canaries build Santo Domingo's first mill with two vertical rollers.
King Manuel recommends a sugar-factory chief for Brazil: the Crown means Brazil to make sugar.
A Chinese report records claying: a roof tile makes sugar 'white as snow'.
Brazilian sugar pays duties in Lisbon and ships in commercial quantities.
Spanish soldiers sack Antwerp and its refining industry collapses.
Portugal passes to Philip II, turning the Dutch revolt into a war on Portuguese shipping.
The Dutch hold the sugar coast of Brazil; Sephardic Jews in their settlements learn sugar-making.
Song Yingxing's treatise illustrates the two-roller crusher and describes claying.

how_to_read: Begin with *Economy* for the numbers and *World* for the politics, then *Exchange* and *Lives* for the people who bore the cost. The *Technology* lane places the Chinese and Atlantic mills side by side.
The Nexus shows how the sack of Antwerp, the Dutch Revolt and Brazil are one causal chain; the next folio picks up with the English and French Caribbean.

sources.intro: From here the folio is built on the standard English-language histories of sugar and colonial economies, with Mazumdar's China as the main non-Atlantic source.
main: Mazumdar, *Sugar and Society in China* (about forty entries), for Chinese, Dutch-Asian and some Atlantic material.
Smith, *Sugar: A Global History*, and Mintz, *Sweetness and Power*, for the Atlantic and the English side.
Walvin, Buttery, Deerr (cited through others) and Eltis for specific points, with Kiple for the Chinese-Atlantic mill question.
contested: The São Tomé revolt of 1595 and its supposed destruction of the industry ([[c3]]).
Who invented the three-roller mill in Brazil ([[te3]]).
gaps: Deerr's *History of Sugar* and the Portuguese sources for Madeira and São Tomé, and a Dutch-Brazil specialist, were not read.
No source for the Java Cultivation System or Cretan cane in this period.
